opus-5.5.text:
I think the thing that really stands out is the combination of ambition and patience. Demis has this ability to pick problems that are genuinely enormous, the kind of thing where, if you crack it, it changes a whole field, and then to commit to them for the long haul. Protein structure prediction is the obvious example. That wasn't a six-month project. It was years of sustained effort, with setbacks along the way, and a real belief that it was the right problem to be working on.

The other part is how he thinks about the problem itself. He's very good at asking, "Is this the kind of problem that AI can actually make a step change on?" He looks for problems that have a clear objective you can measure, lots of data or a good simulator, and a huge search space that humans can't navigate by intuition alone. When you have those ingredients, you can bring the full force of machine learning to bear. That framing has shaped a lot of how I think about choosing problems, including in drug discovery.

And then there's the culture. He brings scientists and engineers together and treats engineering as a first-class part of doing science. At DeepMind you'd have world-class researchers sitting next to world-class engineers, all pointed at one mission, rather than lots of people running small independent projects. That "Apollo program" style of organizing research is quite rare in academia, and I think it's a big reason why things like AlphaGo and AlphaFold actually happened.

He also has a real sense of the narrative arc of science. He's not just optimizing for the next paper. He's thinking about what the field needs, where the frontier is going to be in five or ten years, and how to get there first. That long-term vision, combined with being very hands-on about the details, is a pretty special mix.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the thing that stood out most to me, having spent the better part of a decade there, is that Demis genuinely thinks like a scientist first and a manager second, and he built the whole organization around that. He has this incredible intuition for which problems are both important and tractable right now, and he's willing to place big bets on them years before the field catches up. AlphaGo was like that, AlphaFold was like that. He'd pick a grand challenge, something that felt almost impossibly ambitious, and then say, okay, let's actually go and do this.

The other piece is the way he structured the research culture. It was very much modeled on the idea of running lots of small, focused teams in parallel, giving them a lot of autonomy, and then at the right moment pulling the pieces together into a bigger effort. So you'd have people exploring quite freely, and then when something started to work, he'd bring the full weight of the organization behind it. That combination of exploration and then really decisive concentration of resources is hard to get right, and he was unusually good at it.

And he was always in the details. He'd come to the reading groups, he'd know what was going on in the individual projects, he'd ask the hard technical questions. That mattered a lot for morale, because people felt that the person at the top actually understood and cared about the science, not just the headlines. For me, as someone who came in from a more academic background, that was really the thing that made DeepMind feel different from anywhere else.

astra-6.text:
What stands out to me is the combination of ambition and scientific depth. Demis can hold a very big vision of where the research could go, but also engage with the details of what would actually make it work. Those are quite different skills, and having both matters.

In research, you need room to explore ideas that might fail, while still having a clear sense of what you're trying to achieve. I think his approach brings those two things together: a willingness to pursue difficult, long-term questions and a focus on making concrete progress toward them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think what stands out is the combination of ambition and scientific intuition. Demis can hold this very long-term vision in his head, but also get into the details and ask the question that really matters: what would we need to demonstrate to know that we’re making progress?

And that’s a difficult balance in research. You need to give people room to explore things that might not work, while maintaining a sense of direction. His commitment to the bigger goal gives that exploration a purpose. You can be working on a very specific problem and still see how it could contribute to something much larger.
